name: Plantar heel pain (plantar fasciitis)
goal: Ease that sharp first-step heel pain, then make the foot and calf strong enough that it stays away. Expect weeks to a few months; steady loading works better than rest.
whoFor: People with plantar heel pain (plantar fasciitis): pain under the heel, worst on the first steps in the morning or after sitting, easing as you warm up.
notFor: Heel pain after a fall or jump that hasn't been checked (possible fracture)
Burning, tingling or numbness in the foot (more likely a nerve)
trackedMetric: Pain on your first steps in the morning (0-10)
painRules: Up to about 3-4 out of 10 during the heel raises is OK if the first-step pain the next morning isn't worse. If it is, drop the load or reps for a few days. Supportive shoes, and avoiding barefoot walking on hard floors, help early on.
redFlags: Heel pain after a fall or jump, or you can't put weight on it
Burning, tingling or numbness in the foot
A hot, red, swollen heel, or fever
Pain in both heels together with morning stiffness or swelling in other joints
Severe pain at night or at rest

phases.name: Calm the morning pain
phases.entryCriteria: Sharp first-step pain in the morning or after sitting.
phases.exitCriteria: First-step pain is easing and double-leg heel raises are comfortable.

items.note: Before your first steps out of bed.

phases.name: High-load strength
phases.exitCriteria: First-step pain is 2 out of 10 or less for 2 weeks.

items.note: Keep it while the mornings are sore.
Start at 3 x 12; after 2 weeks 4 x 10; after 4 weeks 5 x 8 with a backpack.

phases.name: Back to full activity
phases.exitCriteria: Walking, running or hiking without heel pain. Keep heel raises twice a week.

items.note: Only if the heel is calm: a step towards running.

references: Rathleff MS, et al. 2015. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12 months follow-up. Scand J Med Sci Sports 25:e292-300.
DiGiovanni BF, et al. 2003. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain. J Bone Joint Surg Am 85:1270-7.
